title: Alicante Housing Market Analysis
text:
The question
What actually drives housing prices in Alicante — size, location, or amenities? Everyone has an intuition about this; few have the numbers. I wanted an answer that came out of data I had collected myself, and that could be checked by anyone else.

title: Alicante Housing Market Analysis
text:
The data
There was no ready-made dataset, so the project starts one step earlier than usual: collecting it. I scraped 1,802 listings from Idealista, Spain’s largest property portal, capturing eleven variables per listing — price, property type, surface area, rooms, floor, agency, and the amenities that agents advertise (garage, sea views, elevator, terrace).
Addresses on a property portal are deliberately vague, so location had to be reconstructed: each listing was geocoded through Nominatim (OpenStreetMap), resolving roughly 87% of them to coordinates. That step is what turned “location” from a text field into something a model could use.
The result is published on Zenodo under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with a DOI, so the analysis below can be reproduced rather than taken on trust.

title: Alicante Housing Market Analysis
text:
The method
The pipeline runs in six stages: scraping with Selenium, cleaning and outlier handling in Pandas, geospatial enrichment with geopy, unsupervised exploration with UMAP, supervised modelling with XGBoost, and formal hypothesis testing.
Two choices are worth explaining. SHAP was used on top of XGBoost because a price model that cannot say why it predicts a price is useless for the people asking the question. And the amenity claims were put through Mann-Whitney U rather than a t-test, because property prices are heavily skewed and do not meet the normality assumption — a detail that quietly invalidates a lot of published property analysis.

title: Alicante Housing Market Analysis
text:
What came out
Surface area dominates, as expected, but not by as much as the market narrative suggests:



Factor
SHAP importance
Reading




Surface area (m²)

Taken together, the two geographic coordinates carry about as much weight as surface area — location is not a tiebreaker in this market, it is a primary driver.
On amenities, listings with a garage are systematically priced higher (Mann-Whitney U, p ≈ 0.000), and the effect holds independently of the other features. UMAP clustering separated the market into distinct segments by property type and geographic zone, which is the part a buyer or an agency would use in practice: the city is not one market but several.

title: How this blog runs your code and still builds in CI
text:
Most static site generators treat code as text to display. I wanted the opposite: posts where the chart is produced by the code shown next to it, so a figure cannot quietly drift away from the analysis that made it.
Quarto does that. A .qmd file is Markdown plus executable blocks, and a rendered page is the result of running them. Jupyter notebooks work too, with no conversion step.

title: How this blog runs your code and still builds in CI
text:
The problem that setup creates
If posts execute Python, the build server needs Python. And not just Python — the same versions of the same libraries, and sometimes the data, or the build fails on a machine that is not mine. That is a brittle dependency to hang a personal site on.
The fix is one line of configuration:
execute:
  freeze: auto
With freeze, Quarto executes code locally and stores the results in _freeze/, which is committed to the repository. Continuous integration then renders the site from those stored results. It installs Quarto and nothing else — no Python, no libraries, no data. Code is re-executed only when I change the document that contains it.
So the environment lives in exactly one place: my machine, pinned with uv.
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["jupyter>=1.1", "pandas>=2.2", "matplotlib>=3.9"]

title: How this blog runs your code and still builds in CI
text:
Proof it actually executes
The figure below is not an image file. It is drawn when this page is rendered, from the SHAP importances of my Alicante housing market analysis — the five features that move property prices the most in that dataset.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

features = ["Sea views", "Elevator", "Longitude", "Latitude", "Surface area (m²)"]
importance = [0.08, 0.08, 0.13, 0.13, 0.31]

SURFACE, SERIES, INK, MUTED = "#fcfcfb", "#2a78d6", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.1), facecolor=SURFACE)
ax.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
bars = ax.barh(features, importance, height=0.55, color=SERIES)

# Direct labels replace the x-axis: five bars do not need a scale.
for bar, value in zip(bars, importance):
    ax.text(value + 0.007, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2, f"{value:.2f}",
            va="center", ha="left", color=MUTED, fontsize=10)

ax.set_xlim(0, 0.37)
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, colors=INK, labelsize=11)
for side in ("top", "right", "bottom"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color("#d8d8d4")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: SHAP importance of the five strongest price drivers in the Alicante housing dataset (1,802 listings).





Surface area dominates, but latitude and longitude together carry just as much weight — in Alicante, location is not a tiebreaker between similar flats, it is a primary driver of price.

section: What the pipeline looks like end to end
text:
What the pipeline looks like end to end

Write a post, run quarto preview, see it execute locally.
Commit the post and _freeze/.
GitHub Actions installs Quarto, renders, and publishes to GitHub Pages.

The build is fast because nothing is computed twice, and it is reproducible because what CI publishes is exactly what I saw locally.

title: ED-Alert
text: Repository Interactive story

title: ED-Alert
text:
The question
Spain has one of the highest early school leaving rates in Europe. The aggregate figure is well known; what is far less clear is which students are at risk, and on what evidence a guidance counsellor could act before a student drops out rather than after.
This project had a specific audience from the start: vocational-training guidance counsellors, who are not statisticians and who need something they can open, explore and use in a meeting.

title: ED-Alert
text:
The data
Three sources, deliberately combined:

PISA 2022 student questionnaires — the international assessment run by the OECD. The source file is a 2 GB SPSS export, which drives most of the preprocessing work.
ELET indicator by autonomous community, to place each Spanish region against the European benchmark.
Spanish Ministry of Education figures on vocational-training dropout.

The target variable, en_riesgo, was constructed from student performance across the three PISA competences, rather than taken off the shelf. That definition is a modelling decision, not a given, and it is the one I would challenge first if someone disagreed with the results.

title: ED-Alert
text:
The method
Context variables in PISA are overwhelmingly categorical — family situation, school resources, attitudes — which rules out the usual correlation-first approach. Multiple Correspondence Analysis was used to reduce that categorical space and reveal natural groupings of students.
Two models were then trained side by side, for different reasons. Logistic regression gives a counsellor something explainable: coefficients that can be defended in a conversation with a family. Random Forest gives better detection. Both were judged on recall in the risk class rather than on overall accuracy, because in this problem a missed at-risk student costs far more than a false alarm.

title: ED-Alert
text:
What came out



Model
Overall accuracy
Recall, risk class




Logistic regression
—
60%


Random Forest
81%
64%



The gap between 81% accuracy and 64% recall is the honest headline here: the model is considerably better at confirming that a student is fine than at catching one who is not. For a screening tool that is the wrong way round, and it is the first thing I would work on with more data.
MCA surfaced coherent student profiles that map onto the risk classification, which matters more than the model scores for the intended use: counsellors recognise the profiles, and recognising them is what turns a number into a conversation.
The whole analysis was delivered as an interactive Tableau story rather than a report, so the audience can filter to their own region and cohort instead of reading about someone else’s.
